triage.name: Ophthalmia neonatorum
triage.reason: Neonatal eye discharge with a clear differential by timing and organism; reachable via history, exam and conjunctival cultures.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'Blood culture' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or poor feeding)

auto-repaired: workup: 'CT orbits with IV contrast' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if orbital cellulitis or abscess is suspected (proptosis, limited extraocular movements, or severe eyelid swelling))

demographics: Occurs in newborns of both sexes
More common where maternal chlamydia and gonorrhea are prevalent

chief_complaints.text: My baby's eye has a lot of yellow goop
The baby's eyelids are swollen shut

hpi.onset: Develops within the first week when gonococcal, usually 24–48 hours; chlamydial conjunctivitis appears later, often 5–14 days
hpi.duration: Usually brought in within 1–3 days of eye symptoms
hpi.progression: Starts with watery discharge and mild redness, then becomes thicker, purulent discharge and eyelid swelling; without treatment can progress to corneal involvement
hpi.location: Both eyes are typically involved, though one may be worse
hpi.quality: Thick, yellow-green discharge; eye pain cannot be reported by infant
hpi.severity: Moderate; can be severe with corneal ulceration if untreated

argues_against: Fever or lethargy suggests systemic infection

atypical.how_it_differs: Chlamydial conjunctivitis has later onset (5–14 days) and less purulent, more watery discharge; gonococcal is earlier and more purulent.

general.mild: Well-appearing neonate with mild eye discharge and redness; otherwise normal activity
general.moderate: Fussy neonate with swollen eyelids, often keeps eyes closed; no systemic signs
general.severe: Irritable, difficult to console; eyelids swollen shut with copious purulent discharge; may have corneal clouding
general.critical: Ill-appearing or lethargic if systemic spread, or with signs of corneal ulceration/perforation

findings.finding: Redness of palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva

findings.maneuver: Shine a penlight across the cornea
Apply fluorescein and examine with blue light
Examine cornea with fluorescein and blue light
Inspect the skin of the eyelids
findings.finding: No vesicular lesions on the eyelids

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected orbital cellulitis or abscess (not routine for conjunctivitis)

initial.test: Conjunctival swab for Gram stain and culture
initial.why: Identifies the organism and provides a rapid Gram stain clue; should be done before antibiotics

initial.test: Conjunctival NAAT for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
initial.why: Highly sensitive and specific; detects both common bacterial causes

initial.test: Maternal NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia
initial.why: Identifies maternal infection and guides treatment of mother and partners

initial.only_if: systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or poor feeding

initial.why: Evaluates for orbital cellulitis or abscess
initial.only_if: orbital cellulitis or abscess is suspected (proptosis, limited extraocular movements, or severe eyelid swelling)

confirmatory.test: Culture on chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin media
confirmatory.why: Confirms the pathogen and provides antibiotic susceptibility for gonorrhea

not_indicated.why: Blood counts are usually normal in isolated conjunctivitis and do not guide therapy
Inflammatory markers are not useful in isolated neonatal conjunctivitis
Not indicated unless there are signs of meningitis or disseminated infection

decision_points: Collect conjunctival specimens before applying topical antibiotics to maximize culture yield
Treat mother and sexual partner if gonorrhea or chlamydia is identified
Urgent ophthalmology consultation for corneal involvement or severe purulent discharge
Systemic antibiotics are required for gonococcal conjunctivitis; topical therapy alone is inadequate

criteria.name: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) diagnosis
criteria.summary: Clinical diagnosis based on timing, eye findings, and laboratory confirmation; no formal scoring system exists.
items: Onset 24–48 hours with profuse purulent discharge suggests gonococcal conjunctivitis
Onset 5–14 days with watery then mucoid discharge suggests chlamydial conjunctivitis
Gram stain of conjunctival exudate shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci in gonococcal disease
NAAT or culture confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis

differential.name: Chemical conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Neonatal eye redness and discharge in the first day of life, often after ocular prophylaxis

history: Symptoms begin within 24 hours of birth and improve by 24-48 hours
History of silver nitrate or antibiotic ointment prophylaxis
exam: Mild conjunctival injection without purulent discharge

differential.name: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Neonatal eye redness with or without vesicular skin lesions; can cause corneal scarring and systemic infection
differential.trigger: Vesicles on the eyelids or a dendritic corneal ulcer

history: Onset usually within first 2 weeks of life
exam: Vesicular lesions on eyelids or elsewhere
labs: PCR of conjunctival swab or vesicle fluid positive for HSV

differential.name: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction
differential.why_considered: Persistent tearing and mattering in a young infant without conjunctival injection

history: Chronic tearing and crusting since birth or first weeks
No acute onset of purulent discharge
exam: Pressure over lacrimal sac may express debris

differential.name: Other bacterial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Purulent eye discharge in a neonate but less severe and later onset than gonococcal

history: Onset after first few days, often after discharge from hospital
exam: Gram stain shows other organisms (e.g., gram-positive cocci)
labs: Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus species

differential.name: Orbital cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Eyelid swelling and erythema with eye discharge can be mistaken for severe conjunctivitis

imaging: CT orbits shows orbital fat stranding, subperiosteal abscess

severity.mild: Watery or slightly mucoid discharge, mild conjunctival redness, no eyelid edema or corneal findings; infant well-appearing
severity.moderate: Purulent discharge, conjunctival injection, and eyelid edema; infant may be fussy but feeding normally; no corneal involvement
severity.severe: Copious purulent discharge, marked eyelid edema, chemosis, and signs of corneal involvement (haze, ulcer); infant may be irritable and feeding poorly

red_flags.meaning: Risk of corneal perforation and permanent vision loss; urgent ophthalmology
Herpes simplex infection with risk of encephalitis and disseminated disease
Systemic dissemination (sepsis, meningitis) requires full sepsis workup

red_flags.finding: Lack of improvement after 48 hours of appropriate therapy
red_flags.meaning: Wrong diagnosis or resistant organism; reassess

complications.name: Chlamydial pneumonia
clues: Occurs in infants with chlamydial conjunctivitis

special_populations.differences: Neonates are at higher risk for systemic dissemination and corneal complications; require systemic rather than topical antibiotics for gonococcal or chlamydial disease, and evaluation for co-infection.

key_questions.question: When did the eye discharge start?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset 24–48 hours suggests gonococcal; 5–14 days suggests chlamydial

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Thick yellow-green purulent discharge vs watery or mucoid discharge

key_questions.question: Did the baby receive eye ointment or drops after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Ocular prophylaxis is usually given; its absence increases risk

key_questions.question: Was the baby delivered vaginally?
key_questions.looking_for: Vaginal delivery exposes the baby to maternal genital flora

key_questions.question: Did you have gonorrhea, chlamydia, or other infections during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal STI is the primary source; positive or untreated infection increases risk

key_questions.question: Has the baby had fever, poor feeding, or unusual sleepiness?
key_questions.looking_for: Absence of fever and lethargy suggests isolated conjunctivitis; presence suggests systemic infection

key_questions.question: Are there any blisters or sores on the eyelids or skin?

reasoning_points: Newborn with acute eye discharge and redness, with onset in first weeks of life
Timing and discharge character differentiate gonococcal (early, purulent) from chlamydial (later, mucoid)
Maternal gonorrhea/chlamydia, vaginal delivery, and lack of ocular prophylaxis are crucial risk factors
Conjunctival Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci in gonococcal disease
NAAT or culture confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis
Must differentiate from chemical conjunctivitis, herpes simplex, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and orbital cellulitis
Systemic antibiotics are required for gonococcal and chlamydial conjunctivitis; topical therapy alone is inadequate
Evaluate for corneal involvement and systemic dissemination, with urgent ophthalmology referral for severe cases

easy: Newborn with profuse purulent discharge at 24–48 hours
Mother known to have untreated gonorrhea
Classic Gram stain with gram-negative intracellular diplococci
medium: Chlamydial conjunctivitis with later onset and less purulent discharge
Chemical conjunctivitis after ocular prophylaxis, onset <24 hours
No known maternal STI, requiring targeted testing
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction with chronic tearing but normal conjunctiva
hard: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis with eyelid vesicles and dendritic ulcer
Systemic signs of sepsis or meningitis from disseminated infection
Mother denies STI but infant has positive gonococcal culture
